title: A broiler, a conglomerate and a write-off
lede: Burger Chef was not beaten by a better hamburger. It was bought by a packaged-food company that expanded it faster than it could find good sites or people, and then spent ten years shrinking it.

chapters.title: A restaurant built to sell a machine
chapters.cap: price of the flame-broiled hamburger in the early years
chapters.body:
The company began as an equipment maker. General Equipment of Indianapolis made frozen custard and soft-serve machines, and in the 1950s Frank Thomas Jr. agreed to mass-produce flame broilers for a Miami-based chain, keeping the right to sell them in every state but Florida.[^6] Local histories say the brothers Frank and Donald Thomas held a patent on the broiler; we could not locate the patent itself.[^6]

In 1957 Frank Thomas opened a pilot hamburger stand at the Little America amusement park in Indianapolis to show the equipment. The grill did not sell. The 15-cent hamburgers did.[^5][^7] The first restaurant called Burger Chef opened in spring 1958 at 1300 West 16th Street, with Robert Wildman as partner.[^5]

Franchising did the rest. An owner’s investment was about $129,000 and the Encyclopedia of Indianapolis puts the average return at 50% a year, a retrospective figure.[^5] There were about 70 restaurants by 1960 and about 500 by 1966.[^5][^6] The burger, fries and shake combination sold for 45 cents, and the double-decker Big Shef arrived in 1964 or 1965, before the Big Mac.[^7][^8]
chapters.artCaption: Original illustration of a conveyor flame broiler. By the mid-1960s the chain’s machine was said to cook about 2,000 burgers an hour.[^8]

chapters.title: General Foods buys the number two
chapters.cap: purchase price in 1968, as reported by The New York Times
chapters.body:
By December 1967 Burger Chef was the second-largest restaurant chain in the United States, behind McDonald’s.[^4][^5] The Thomas brothers concluded that they lacked the resources of their rivals and sold.[^6] General Foods, the maker of Maxwell House and Jell-O, paid $16 million in 1968 for about 700 owned and franchised units.[^1] Other accounts give the price as $16.5 million, nearly $20 million or $25 million, and the unit count as anything from 650 to nearly 900.[^5][^6][^7][^9]

The new owner expanded at once. The 1,000th restaurant opened in 1969.[^4] General Foods also bought a roast-beef chain started by a Burger Chef franchisee for $3 million and renamed it Rix. Together the two reached 1,200 outlets.[^1] Time puts the Burger Chef peak at 1,200 restaurants in 1971, about 100 fewer than McDonald’s had.[^4]

The people who had built the chain did not stay. The founder left, another senior executive had a heart attack, and within two years the management turnover was “nearly total.”[^1] General Foods supplied replacements from its own ranks.

chapters.title: Too far, too fast
chapters.cap: loss General Foods disclosed in January 1972, most of it on Burger Chef
chapters.body:
In January 1972 General Foods disclosed that it had lost $83 million, mostly on Burger Chef. After tax the extraordinary loss came to $46.8 million, of which $39 million was charged to fast food. Earnings per share fell from $2.38 to $1.32.[^1] A later Times article rounds the write-off to $80 million before tax.[^2]

The company’s own explanation was real estate. It had made “inflated property commitments in weak marketing areas,” in the words of the Times, and it had staffed a restaurant business with packaged-goods managers.[^1] Arthur E. Larkin Jr., the president of General Foods, retired abruptly in April 1972 at 55.

The remedy was retreat. All the Rix units were closed. More than 100 Burger Chef units had shut by June 1972 and a net reduction of 25% was planned, with the chain to be consolidated into a regional one.[^1]

pull.text: We moved too far, too fast, under the pressures of the times.
pull.who: Arthur E. Larkin Jr., former president of General Foods, The New York Times, June 11, 1972[^1]

chapters.title: Good ideas in a shrinking chain
chapters.cap: the Funmeal, six years before the McDonald’s Happy Meal
chapters.body:
The smaller chain kept inventing. A “Quality Improvement Plan” brought grilled buns and trials of salad bars, and the Works Bar let customers dress their own burgers.[^6][^9] In 1973 came the Funmeal, a boxed children’s meal with puzzles and stories built around the mascots Burger Chef and Jeff.[^8][^17] In 1978 the box carried Star Wars: seven different Funmeal trays with punch-out toys.[^19]

McDonald’s launched the Happy Meal in 1979.[^20] The Indianapolis Star records that Burger Chef sued McDonald’s over it, and in 1981 sued Burger King over a “Fun School Meal,” a case settled out of court.[^7] Later accounts say the McDonald’s suit was dismissed. We found no court record, so the outcome is **unverified**.[^18]

The decade also brought the event for which the name is now most often searched. On the night of November 17, 1978, four young employees, Jayne Friedt, Ruth Shelton, Daniel Davis and Mark Flemmonds, were abducted from the restaurant in Speedway, Indiana. They were found dead two days later. The case has never been solved.[^15][^16]

By the end of the 1970s the system had a little over 650 restaurants.[^5]

chapters.title: Hardee’s buys the buildings
chapters.cap: approximate price agreed with Hardee’s in December 1981
chapters.body:
In March 1981 the Times described Burger Chef as “barely a breakeven operation.”[^2] On December 10 it reported that General Foods had agreed to sell the unit to Hardee’s Food Systems, a subsidiary of Imasco of Montreal, for about $44 million. The chairman of General Foods said the business was “not central to the long-term direction” of the company.[^3]

The sale was completed in 1982; we have not found the closing date.[^10] On November 15, 1982 an Indianapolis station reported on 75 local restaurants becoming Hardee’s. Hardee’s chairman expected about 2,100 units in 38 states.[^10] The Indianapolis Star puts the company-owned restaurants converted at nearly 260, with franchisees given the option.[^7]

Some franchisees kept the name for years. The last, in Cookeville, Tennessee, became a “Pleasers” restaurant in 1996.[^4]
